_about: The alphabet key: both printed accounts of Bogoras's notation, transcribed. Read by harness/alphabet.py; served as the `alphabet` run over scan 1-030, which is the leaf the p. 10 key is printed on. This store holds only what the pages say — the glyphs, their glosses, and the grid Mythology arranges them in. What each sort is worth in IPA is `harness/ipa.py`'s (RULES), what a modern description calls the same sound is `ipa.MODERN`'s, and the codepoints are also `keying_spec.md` §2.1-2.3's, which is the inventory's owner. The last of those is a deliberate second statement of one fact: `test_alphabet.py` checks the two against each other rather than merging them, so a drift is a gate failure instead of a silent divergence.

_shape.keys: the printed accounts. `key` is a page of this corpus and carries a ref; `myth` is another volume and carries none, which is why it is marked external.
_shape.grids: Mythology's own arrangement, folio 3. Rows are its labels, verbatim. **Columns are unlabelled in the print and are not named here** — the positions are preserved because they carry his analysis, and naming them stop/affricate/fricative/nasal would be inventing one he did not write. `null` is an empty cell.
_shape.sorts: one entry per printed sort, keyed on this edition's own spelling of it so the join with `ipa.RULES` is by identity rather than by shape. `ref`/`folio` are the leaf and folio it is printed on, which for every sort here is 1-030 and 10 — Mythology's set is a subset of p. 10's.
_shape.notes: the running prose below Mythology's key, folio 4. Rules about how forms are said rather than about the notation.

source.what: Alphabet, Bogoras, The Chukchee, part 1 front matter
caveats: Mythology's account was read from page images in scratch/, not from a scan in this corpus. It is a different volume and has no ref here.
Four sorts (ë, ḷ, ṛ, š) have a gloss and no IPA value in ipa.RULES, because turning a gloss into a symbol is a judgement rather than a lookup. They are entries here with `ipa: false`.
The fourth member of the spirant series is damaged in the print (keying_spec.md §2.5 F10) and is recorded as unread rather than inferred from the series.

keys.opening: The following alphabet has been used for transcribing Chukchee sounds: —
keys.note: A reduced notation. Its sorts are a subset of p. 10's — it has no ë, ḷ, ṛ, g, x, x˙, š, c or j and no spirant series — but it is the only one of the two that arranges them, and its glosses are fuller.

vowels.note: Three rows and no row labels in the print. The arrangement is the analysis: ä, ê and ɵ sit over a, e and o as their long counterparts, and ŭ sits under u with the obscure short series rather than beside it.

consonants.note: **His place names are one step back from modern usage, and this is the most useful thing on the page.** `k` and `ñ` are on his Palatal row and `q`, `g̣`, `h` on his Velar row — so his "velar" is what a modern description calls uvular and his "palatal" is what it calls velar. The Alveolar block runs three lines: palatalized, then the affricates and ř, then the plain series.

rules.text: Extra long and extra short vowels are indicated by the macron and breve respectively.
The diphthongs are formed by combining any of the vowels with i and u.
Very long and very short vowels are indicated by the macron and breve respectively.
The diphthongs are formed by combining any of the vowels with i and u.

notes.text: wkw (before and after u, — kw) is pronounced as a compound sound. The lips are placed in u position, while k is formed by the back of the tongue.
In a similar way g̣u and g̣o are often pronounced with a faint w sound between consonant and vowel.
ɪ terminal and unaccented is often pronounced with a slight nasal sound.
In a few cases w in the beginning of the word is also pronounced with a nasal sound. No additional signs have been used to indicate the nasal character of these sounds.
i (consonantic y) between vowels is generally omitted or pronounced very faintly.
yɪ when preceded by the vowels e and i almost always loses its consonantic character and becomes i. For instance: geiˊlqäʟin instead of ge-yɪˊlqäʟin.

The terminal sound is often modified by the initial sound of the following word, according to certain phonetic rules. These will be given in a discussion of the Chukchee grammar. Owing to the slowness of speech necessary for writing from dictation many such changes have disappeared in the texts as taken down by me. I have thought it advisable to leave these cases uncorrected.
